alternative: Compute the payload outside the constructor-initializer chain and hand it in: a static factory or helper (or a constructor parameter) passed to base(...), with the same value stored in the derived type's field afterwards - or replace inheritance with composition and hold the stream/buffer as a field the derived type owns. C# forbids referencing this or any instance member in a constructor initializer, and classes have a single base, so there is no second base to carry the based-member.
idiom_name: none - base(...) cannot read instance state and there is no second class base
implementation_notes: C# has the trap and none of the escape hatch. The language specification is explicit: 'An instance constructor initializer cannot access the instance being created', so it is a compile-time error to reference this in an argument expression of base(...) or to reference any instance member by simple name - even though the documented initialization sequence runs the most derived type's field initializers before the base type's field initializers and base constructors, an argument in the base initializer still cannot name the field. Nor can the member be relocated into a helper base, because a C# class has exactly one direct base class and interfaces carry no instance state - which is precisely the structural hole the C++ idiom fills. What replaces it is a value produced before delegation: a static helper whose result is passed to base(...) (the same value is then assigned to the field), a private this(...) constructor that takes the payload as a parameter and re-exposes it, or composition when the inheritance was incidental.
pitfalls: The payload must travel as an argument, not as a field: the derived field is still null while base code runs if the assignment happens after delegation, and reading it from the base constructor sees the default value (the specification's 'the value of y is 0' example) rather than the object's data.

A virtual member invoked from the base constructor runs before the derived field assignment and before the derived constructor body, so the derived-side state it touches is default-initialised even though field initializers (which run earlier) may have set it.
Passing the payload twice - once to base(...) and once into the field - invites drift the moment one of the two computations changes; the constructor chain must be the only place that creates it.
Replacing inheritance with composition changes the public surface (members must be forwarded), so it is a design decision and not a local refactor.
